0.title: Faith for Young Adults
0.essay:
Between about eighteen and thirty, more big decisions are made than in any other stretch of life: where to study or work, whom to marry, which church to join, what to do with money and time. Many young adults also drift from the faith in these years. This study is about being faithful to Christ as you set the direction of your life.

A season of freedom

For the first time, no one is making you go to church. You choose your friends, your hours and your habits. That freedom is a gift, and a test. What you do with it will shape the rest of your life. “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come” (Ecclesiastes 12:1).

The chapters

1. Leaving Home with Your Faith: university, the drift and finding a church. 2. What Should I Do with My Life?: calling, career and decisions. 3. Singleness, Dating and Marriage. 4. Money, Work and Independence. 5. Doubt, Ideas and the Culture. 6. Church, Friendship and Loneliness.

For reflection

What decisions are in front of you at the moment? Which of them would you most like God’s wisdom for?

1.title: Leaving Home with Your Faith
1.essay:
Leaving home, for university, work or a new city, is a turning point. Some young Christians flourish. Many quietly drift. The difference is rarely a dramatic crisis. It is usually the habits of the first few weeks.

How the drift happens

Few people decide to abandon Christ. Instead, they miss church one Sunday because they were out late, then another because they have work. They do not find Christian friends. Prayer and Bible reading fade. A year later, they no longer feel like Christians. Hebrews warns, “we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it” (Hebrews 2:1).

The first three weeks

Find a church in your first week, not your first term. Look for one that preaches the Bible faithfully, and commit to it, rather than trying a new place each Sunday. Join a student Christian group if there is one, but do not let it replace the church. Introduce yourself to the pastor. Join a small group. Say yes when an older family invites you for lunch.

Making faith your own

Without your parents and youth leaders, your faith needs its own roots. Set a time each day for Scripture and prayer, even fifteen minutes. Read one good Christian book each term. Find a Christian friend who will ask you how you are really doing.

New freedom, old temptations

Alcohol, sex, and late nights are part of the culture of many universities and workplaces. You do not have to join in. Decide ahead of time what you will and will not do, and find friends who will help you. “Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart” (2 Timothy 2:22). Note the last phrase: you need companions.

If you have already drifted

If this describes you, it is not too late. The father in Jesus’ parable ran to meet his returning son (Luke 15:20). Come back to Christ. Find a church this Sunday. Tell someone you want to start again.

A Tuesday afternoon

In her first week at university, Hannah set an alarm for Sunday morning and walked to a church she had found online. Afterwards, a couple invited her and two other students for lunch. Three years later, she was leading a Bible study for first-year students herself.

For reflection

If you have recently moved, have you committed to a church yet? If not, what is stopping you?

2.title: What Should I Do with My Life?
2.essay:
Many young adults feel paralysed by the question of what they should do with their lives. They fear missing God’s will. The Bible’s answer is both more freeing and more demanding than a secret plan to discover.

God’s will

The Bible speaks of God’s will in two ways. There is his sovereign will, his plan for everything, which we do not know in advance (Deuteronomy 29:29). And there is his revealed will, what he commands in Scripture, which we are called to obey. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). The main thing God wants you to do with your life is to love him, trust Christ and grow in holiness, wherever you are.

Making decisions

Within God’s revealed will, you have real freedom. You can choose between good options. God will not usually tell you which job or city to choose by a voice or a sign. Instead, he gives wisdom. Pray. Study what Scripture says. Look at your gifts and what you enjoy. Ask wise Christians what they see in you. Consider where you can serve and where there is a good church. Then decide, and trust God with the outcome. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

Calling and career

Your calling is not only your job. You are called to be a Christian, a church member, a son or daughter, perhaps a spouse and parent, and a neighbour. Your work is one part of that. Any honest work can be done for God (Colossians 3:23). Do not assume that only pastors and missionaries do “real” ministry. But do consider whether God is giving you gifts and a desire for full-time ministry or mission, and talk to your church leaders if so.

The fear of missing out

Our culture tells young adults to keep every option open: to travel, to try everything, to avoid commitment. But a life of open options can become a life of nothing. At some point you must commit to a place, a church, a work and, perhaps, a person. Faithfulness grows in committed soil.

When things go wrong

You may not get the job, or the course may not work out. That is not proof you have missed God’s will. Joseph was sold, falsely accused and forgotten in prison, yet God was working all along (Genesis 50:20). “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

A Tuesday afternoon

Tom had two job offers and had prayed for weeks for a sign. His pastor asked him which one gave him a better church, a better use of his gifts, and fewer temptations. The answer was clear within ten minutes. “I think I was waiting for God to decide so I wouldn’t have to,” Tom said.

For reflection

Is there a decision you are putting off because you are afraid of getting it wrong? What would it mean to decide wisely and trust God with the result?

3.title: Singleness, Dating and Marriage
3.essay:
For many young adults, the question of marriage is never far away. Some long for it, some fear it, some avoid it. God has wise things to say, both to those who marry and to those who do not.

Singleness is not second best

Jesus was single. So was Paul, who called singleness a gift that frees a person to give the Lord “undivided devotion” (1 Corinthians 7:35). Singleness is not a waiting room for real life. It is a real calling, for a season or for life. Use it: serve, build friendships, and invest in the church. And the church must be a family to its single members, not just a place for couples.

Longing for marriage

Yet many singles long to marry, and that is a good desire. “He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD” (Proverbs 18:22). Bring that longing to God honestly. Do not let it become an idol, as if your life cannot begin until you marry. And do not let it make you settle for someone who does not share your faith.

Whom to marry

The Bible gives one clear rule: marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39), that is, a Christian. Within that, look for character: someone who loves Christ, is humble, kind, honest and faithful, and will help you grow. Attraction matters, but it is not enough. Watch how they treat others, how they handle anger, money and family, and what they do with their time. Ask your friends and older Christians what they see.

Dating

Date with purpose. A relationship should be heading towards marriage, or towards a wise, kind ending. Be honest about your intentions. Keep sexual purity, which means not living together or sleeping together before marriage. That is hard in our culture, but it is God’s good design, and it protects you both. Involve your church and family. A relationship hidden from everyone is a warning sign.

Marriage

Marriage is a covenant before God, not a contract that lasts while feelings last. It is a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Prepare for it: get premarital counselling, talk about money, children, roles and conflict, and be realistic. And marriage will not solve your loneliness or your sin. Two sinners will need much grace.

Sexual sin and grace

If you have already sinned sexually, there is forgiveness. “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). Repent, receive his grace and begin again. Your past need not define your future.

A Tuesday afternoon

Priya was twenty-eight and tired of being asked when she would marry. She decided to stop waiting for her life to begin. She took on a role in her church’s children’s work, started hosting a monthly meal, and planned a mission trip. She still hoped to marry. But she no longer felt she was wasting her life.

For reflection

Whether single or dating, are you using this season to serve Christ, or just waiting for the next one?

4.title: Money, Work and Independence
4.essay:
For many young adults, the first pay packet brings a new freedom and new temptations. The habits you form now, with money, work and time, will likely stay with you for life.

Your first job

Your first job may not be your dream job. Do it well anyway. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). Be punctual, honest and willing to learn. Treat your boss and colleagues with respect. Faithfulness in small things leads to more responsibility (Luke 16:10).

Budgeting

A budget is not a restriction, but a plan for faithfulness. Know what comes in and what goes out. Spend less than you earn. Save regularly, even a little. “The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty” (Proverbs 21:5).

Debt

Many young adults carry student loans, credit cards or car payments. Some debt is hard to avoid. But be very careful with consumer debt. “The borrower is the slave of the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). Avoid buying now and paying later for things you do not need. If you are already in debt, make a plan to pay it off, and seek help if you need it.

Giving

Start giving from your first pay packet, before anything else. Many Christians use the tithe, a tenth, as a starting point. Others give a set proportion and increase it as income grows. “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Giving is easier to start when the amounts are small. It breaks the power of money over you.

Contentment

Social media shows you friends on holiday, buying flats and getting promotions. Comparison breeds discontent. “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6). Be content with what you have, and do not measure your life by your income or possessions.

Rest

Young adults often overwork, or let work spill into every evening. Keep a rhythm of rest and worship each week. Your worth is not in your productivity.

A Tuesday afternoon

On the day his first salary arrived, Josh set up three automatic payments: one to his church, one to a savings account and one for his rent. Only then did he look at what was left. It was less than he had hoped, but he never felt the pressure his friends did at the end of the month.

For reflection

If someone looked at your bank statement, what would they say you treasure?

5.title: Doubt, Ideas and the Culture
5.essay:
In your twenties you will meet ideas that challenge your faith, in lectures, at work and online. Some young Christians “deconstruct” their faith and never rebuild it. Others come through stronger. The difference often lies in how honestly they face the questions.

A secular age

In much of the West, belief in God is no longer assumed. Many of your friends will see Christianity as outdated, intolerant or simply irrelevant. That can make faith feel fragile. But Christianity has always been a minority faith in hostile cultures. It began that way.

Hard questions

You will hear objections: that science has replaced God, that the Bible is unreliable, that Christianity is oppressive, that suffering disproves a good God, and that all religions are equally valid. These are serious questions, and they have serious answers. Read widely and carefully. Christians have thought about these things for two thousand years. Be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15).

Deconstruction

Some people use “deconstruction” to mean carefully examining what they were taught, to separate what is biblical from what was merely cultural. That can be healthy. Others use it to mean taking apart their faith altogether. Often this begins with real hurt: a church that was harsh, a leader who fell, or questions that were never allowed. If that is your story, your pain is real. But do not let the failures of Christians lead you away from Christ himself. When many left Jesus, Peter said, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68).

Sexuality and ethics

The sharpest disagreement between the church and the culture today is over sexuality and gender. Many young Christians feel ashamed of what the Bible teaches, or fear losing friends. Study the Bible’s teaching for yourself, and understand why it is good, not just what it says. And hold it with love. You can have friends who disagree with you, and you can stand firm without being harsh.

Feeding your mind

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The culture is shaping you every day, through what you watch, read and scroll. Let Scripture and good Christian books shape you more. Find an older Christian who has thought about these questions and can walk with you.

A Tuesday afternoon

In her second year at university, Anna read a book that made her question everything. Instead of hiding it, she told her pastor. They read it together, chapter by chapter, alongside a Christian response. She said afterwards, “I came out with fewer certainties about some secondary things, and much more certainty about Jesus.”

For reflection

What question about the faith most troubles you? Who could you explore it with honestly?

6.title: Church, Friendship and Loneliness
6.essay:
Young adulthood can be surprisingly lonely. Friends move away, routines change and social media can make you feel connected while leaving you isolated. God’s answer to loneliness is not only marriage or a career, but his family, the church.

Commit to a church

Many young adults treat church as an option among many: they attend when it suits them, or watch online. But the church is Christ’s body, and you are a part of it. “Not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:25). Become a member. Serve. Give. Show up even when you do not feel like it. Committed people make friends; occasional visitors do not.

Friendship

Deep friendship takes time and intention. Invite people to your home, even if it is small. Eat together. Ask real questions. Be honest about your struggles. “A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). Look for friends of all ages, not just your own.

Loneliness

If you are lonely, you are not alone in that. Many in their twenties feel the same, though few admit it. Bring it to God, who “settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6). Then take a small step: join a small group, invite someone for coffee, volunteer. Loneliness often eases when we start serving others.

Mentors

Find an older Christian who can walk with you. Paul told older women to train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), and he himself mentored Timothy. Ask someone to meet with you every few weeks to read the Bible and pray. Most mature Christians will be glad to be asked.

Serving

Your twenties are a wonderful time to serve. You may have more energy and flexibility now than you will later. Help with children or youth, welcome newcomers, join the music team, go on a mission trip. Do not wait until you feel ready.

A Tuesday afternoon

David moved to a new city for work and knew no one. For two months, he went home straight after church. Then he started staying for coffee and helping to stack chairs. One of the other chair-stackers invited him to a small group. Within a year, that group had become his closest friends.

For reflection

Are you a committed member of a church, or just an attender? What is one step you could take this week to build friendships there?
